title: Strata Clean Energy — Technology Study Guide

sections.title: Start here: the seller at the table
ps: In September 2025 GridStor bought a 100 MW / 400 MWh Arizona battery with a 20-year utility {{tolling agreement}} attached, from a company that had won the contract, signed the battery supplier and never intended to own it. This guide teaches that company's side of the table: the {{originator}} that turns land, a grid position and a utility {{RFP}} win into a project a fund will pay for, sells it before the toll begins, and keeps a fee. It teaches what a buyer is actually paying for, why a founder-owned developer sells a 20-year contract it could have kept, how the {{development margin}} and the retained service contracts replace an owner's cash flow, and where the model breaks.

**What it deliberately does not repeat:** the GridStor guide reads the same transaction from the buyer's chair — what a sponsor-created platform pays for and how it contracts before it builds; the Aypa guide teaches the contracted platform as an asset a buyer prices; the Spearmint guide teaches the merchant developer and the pre-COD market at transmission scale; the Available Power guide teaches selling small batteries at notice to proceed with a turnkey EPC. The Classroom owns tolling, ancillary stacking and duration arithmetic. Here the battery is a product the developer makes and sells, and the question is what the product is.

**One idea carries the guide.** A contract is worth more to the owner who can hold it longest at the lowest cost of capital. A founder-owned developer with a bank revolver cannot hold a 20-year toll as cheaply as a EUR 12 billion infrastructure fund can, so it sells the toll to the fund and gets paid for having created it.

sections.title: What the originator makes
ps: A developer that builds to sell is a manufacturer whose product is a de-risked project. The raw materials are a site with a willing landowner, a {{queue position}} that becomes an {{interconnection agreement}}, county and state permits, a utility contract, and a battery supply agreement. Each one removes a reason the project could fail, and a buyer pays for the removed reasons — the rungs of the {{development stage ladder}} — rather than for the megawatts.

**The contract is the rung that matters most.** Strata's three flagship batteries were all won in utility procurements: Ventura in Southern California Edison's resource-adequacy solicitation (a 20-year {{RA contract}}, approved by the CPUC in December 2019), Scatter Wash and White Tank in Arizona Public Service's all-source RFPs of 2022 and 2023 (20-year tolls). A toll or an RA contract converts a battery's uncertain hourly earnings into a fixed payment from a regulated utility, which is exactly the cash flow an {{infrastructure fund}} exists to buy.

**The supply agreement is the rung that proves the schedule.** White Tank's Canadian Solar e-STORAGE supply agreement and 20-year {{LTSA}} were signed in March 2025, six months before the sale to GridStor. The buyer inherited a project with its battery, its price and its service contract fixed — a project whose remaining risks were construction and a substation, not procurement in a tariff year.

**The financing rung is optional.** Scatter Wash had already closed a USD 559 million construction and tax-equity financing (J.P. Morgan, Nomura, U.S. Bancorp Impact Finance and five more lenders) when Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners bought it in September 2024. A financed, contracted project under construction is the top of the ladder short of operation; White Tank was sold a rung lower, contracted and procured but not yet financed. The price a buyer pays for each rung is never published — Strata disclosed no sale price for any of the three — so the {{development margin}} is inferred, not read.

sections.title: Why a founder-owned developer sells a 20-year contract
ps: A 20-year toll is a bond-like asset: fixed payments from a regulated utility, low risk once built. The price an owner will pay for it depends on the owner's cost of capital — an infrastructure fund raising money from pensions at single-digit returns can pay more for the same contract than a company that funds itself with a bank {{revolving credit facility}} and its founders' equity. The gap between those two prices is the {{development margin}} the seller collects.

**Strata has no sponsor.** Its financing page says it is 'a 100% privately held company owned by our founders'; the USD 150 million Blackstone put in during 2021 was credit, in the CFO's own words. Its growth capital is three successive revolvers — USD 170 million (Zions, 2022), USD 300 million (Nomura and First Citizens, 2023), USD 450 million (July 2026) — and project-level debt. A revolver funds development and construction; it does not fund owning 1 GWh of batteries for 20 years. A {{family office}} could hold the asset, but only by tying up equity the development business needs.

**Selling is {{capital recycling}}.** The USD 559 million Scatter Wash financing and the equity behind it came back to Strata when CIP bought the project seven months later, and the revolver was upsized twice afterwards. Each sale funds the next RFP bid. The company's own claim that it 'retain[s] ownership in more than 50% of the projects we develop' is true of its North Carolina and Virginia solar base — about 1 GW of owned assets under long-term PPAs — and not of its utility-scale batteries, three of which were sold and one kept.

**The buyer's identity tells the seller's story.** Capital Dynamics was a fund manager; CIP's CI V fund had a EUR 12 billion target; GridStor is a company Goldman Sachs Asset Management created to own contracted batteries. Every buyer was a vehicle with cheaper, longer money than a developer's. That is the whole trade: the originator manufactures a contract, the fund holds it.

sections.title: How the lender reads a project that changes hands
ps: Project debt is lent to the project company, not to its owner, so a sale of the company transfers the loan with it — subject to the lenders' consent. At Scatter Wash the USD 559 million financing closed in February 2024 and the project was sold in September; the lenders' underwriting did not change, because the toll, the EPC and the battery supply were the same. What changed was the equity behind them, from a founder-owned developer to a EUR 12 billion fund — an improvement in the lenders' eyes.

**The {{DSCR}} is set by the contract, not the owner.** A 20-year APS toll produces a fixed revenue line; lenders size the debt so that revenue covers debt service with a margin. That sizing is identical whoever owns the equity, which is why an originator can raise the financing and then sell the financed project: the financing is a feature of the product.

**Tax equity travels too.** U.S. Bancorp Impact Finance was Scatter Wash's 'primary tax-equity investor'; the {{ITC}} belongs to the project's owner at placement in service, so the buyer inherits both the credit and the tax-equity partner. On the two Vermont batteries Strata kept, it raised USD 8.7 million of {{tax equity}} itself — among the first standalone-storage credits monetised under the IRA.

**What the corporate lender underwrites is different.** Strata's revolver lenders (Nomura, First Citizens, ING and five unnamed banks under {{Green Loan Principles}}) look at the pipeline, the EPC and O&M cash flows and the owned solar fleet — the recurring business — and at the sale proceeds that repay development spend. The CFO's stated use of the July 2026 upsizing is 'to invest in our development pipeline and support our EPC and O&M businesses': the revolver is working capital for a manufacturer of projects.

sections.title: Sell or hold: the originator's chair
sections.intro: An originator that has just won a 20-year toll chooses between selling the project and holding it. The cards read the trade from the developer's seat; the buyer's seat is the GridStor guide.

cards.t: Sell the contracted project (Scatter Wash, White Tank)
cards.meta: Realise the development margin now; keep a service fee
adv: Equity comes back within months and funds the next RFP bid — growth without a sponsor
The buyer's cheaper capital sets the price, so the seller captures the gap between two costs of capital
Construction and asset-management fees keep a recurring income from an asset no longer on the balance sheet
No 20-year exposure to the toll counterparty, the LTSA or battery degradation
dis: The operating cash flow — the part of the value a fund pays a premium for — goes to the buyer for two decades
Sale prices are never disclosed, so the margin cannot be benchmarked and the seller cannot prove it was paid fairly
A sold project no longer counts as owned: the 'over 50% retained' claim narrows to the solar base
The buyer inherits the supplier and the counterparty relationships the seller built

cards.t: Hold and operate (Justice, Inland Empire, Vermont)
cards.meta: Own the toll for its life on a founder-owned balance sheet
adv: Twenty years of fixed utility revenue and the tax credit stay with the developer
The owned fleet is the collateral and the recurring earnings the corporate lenders look at
Operating experience — the integrator failure at Inland Empire led to Strata's own control platform
dis: Ties up equity the development business needs; a revolver cannot fund long-dated ownership
A founder-owned holder pays more for capital than a fund, so the same contract is worth less held than sold
Concentration: Justice would be the company's largest owned asset by far, in one utility's territory
No sponsor to backstop a construction overrun or a delayed COD

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The buyer disappears.** The model needs a fund with cheaper capital wanting exactly this contract at exactly this stage. If fund appetite for tolled storage weakens — higher rates, a sponsor pulling back, FEOC uncertainty on the supplier — the originator holds a project it did not build its balance sheet to hold. Strata's revolver funds development, not ownership; a project with no buyer becomes the second Justice.

**The contract is the product, and the utility writes it.** Strata's three tolls came from APS's all-source RFPs. A utility that changes its procurement — fewer RFPs, shorter terms, self-build, a rival winning — cuts the supply of the product. The named peers in the same RFPs (Recurrent Energy, EDF Renewables) are bidding for the same tolls.

**Fees are not ownership.** Construction-management and asset-management agreements pay for administration and carry reputational risk; they end when the buyer chooses. 'Under management' figures (4.2 GW in 2024, '260+ assets' in 2026) describe contracts, not assets, and the company switched from gigawatts to asset counts in 2026 without explaining why.

**Siting risk lands on the originator alone.** The rungs a buyer pays for are the ones a county can refuse. Strata's Virginia solar record — Hanover denied unanimously in 2024, Culpeper denied in 2026, Halifax approved 6-2 — is the cost of origination that no sale recovers.

**The record has holes a buyer would want filled.** No sale price for three flagship batteries, no completion release for Justice five months after its stated April 2026 date, an owned fleet the company never breaks out by ISO, site statistics that disagree with each other (285 versus 300+ projects; 1.8 versus 5 GWh of storage developed), and unverified snippets about attrition and stormwater citations. A seller's credibility is part of the product.

cards.q: What does a buyer of a late-stage battery project actually pay for?
cards.a: The risks the originator has already retired — site, interconnection, permits, the utility contract, the supply agreement, sometimes the financing — not the megawatts. Each rung of the development ladder is a reason the project can no longer fail.

cards.q: Why is a 20-year utility toll worth more to an infrastructure fund than to a founder-owned developer?
cards.a: The fund's capital is cheaper and longer-dated: it raises money from pensions at single-digit returns and holds assets for decades. A developer funding itself with a bank revolver values the same fixed cash flow at a higher discount rate, so the fund pays more.

cards.q: What is the development margin and when is it earned?
cards.a: The gap between what the originator spent to reach a saleable stage and the sale price. It is earned on sale, not on operation, and it is almost never disclosed — Strata published no price for Ventura, Scatter Wash or White Tank.

cards.q: What is capital recycling for a developer without a sponsor?
cards.a: Selling a finished or late-stage project to release the equity tied up in it and fund the next bids. Strata's revolver funds development; the sale proceeds replace the equity a sponsor would otherwise supply.

cards.q: Does a project financing survive a sale of the project?
cards.a: Yes, with lender consent: the loan sits with the project company and is sized on the contract's revenue (the DSCR), not the owner. Scatter Wash's USD 559 million financing closed in February 2024 and the project was sold in September.

cards.q: What is a construction-management agreement and what risk does it carry?
cards.a: A fee contract to manage the EPC, schedule and budget for the new owner. The EPC keeps fixed-price risk and the owner keeps overrun risk above it; the manager earns a fee and carries reputational risk. Strata holds one at Scatter Wash for CIP.

cards.q: What does 'assets under management' mean for a developer that sells its projects?
cards.a: Service contracts, not ownership. Strata reports '260+' PV and BESS assets under O&M management; the batteries it sold appear there, the ones it owns appear in 'nearly 1 GW of owned assets'.

cards.q: Why does the supply agreement matter to a buyer of an unbuilt battery?
cards.a: It fixes the battery's price, delivery and service terms before the sale, so the buyer's remaining risk is construction rather than procurement. White Tank's Canadian Solar agreement and 20-year LTSA were signed six months before GridStor bought the project.

cards.q: What is the largest single risk to the originate-and-sell model?
cards.a: That the buyer disappears — a fund market that stops wanting tolled storage at that stage. The developer is then holding a project its balance sheet was not built to hold.

cards.q: Where does the utility fit in this model?
cards.a: It manufactures the product's core: the all-source RFP that produces the 20-year toll. Fewer RFPs, shorter terms or a rival bidder winning cut off the supply of saleable projects.

items.q: Which party's cost of capital sets the price a fund pays for a tolled battery?
items.why: The buyer discounts the contract's fixed cash flows at its own cost of capital; the gap between that and the seller's is the development margin.

items.q: What did Strata keep after selling Scatter Wash to CIP?
items.why: CIP's release: 'Strata will continue to serve as construction and asset manager'; the equipment O&M sits with Tesla and Novasource.
